title: The Sustainability Series: Unlocking AI for Accessibility with Amy Aisha Brown
description: Send us Fan Mail Unlock the secrets of how AI can transform our world into a more inclusive and accessible place with Amy Aisha Brown from King's College London. Gain invaluable insights into how enhanced accessibility benefits not only individuals with disabilities but also the wider society, particularly as we age. Learn how AI is revolutionizing learning environments and making everyday experiences more navigable for everyone. Discover the practical applications of AI tools that are already making a difference in our daily lives. From Be My (AI Eyes) to Text-to-Signlanguage, from the advanced captioning features of Microsoft Teams to ChatGPT's ability to provide helpful prompts for the neurodivergent, we highlight how AI is improving both personal and professional interactions. We explore the potential of AI in areas like online counseling and apps like Character AI, with unique bespoke AI personalities, making digital experiences more efficient and comfortable for users. We don't shy away from the ethical and societal implications of AI in accessibility. This episode dives into the complexities of bias, privacy concerns, technological dependence, vulnerability and the need for robust regulations. We emphasize the importance of political engagement to ensure AI developments align with human values. Tune in for a balanced discussion on the promises and pitfalls of AI, and why maintaining human-centered options is crucial in our rapidly evolving digital landscape. Speech Accessibility Project (illinois.edu) Be My Eyes - See the world together
summary: Amy Aisha Brown, a learning technologist at King's College London, joins the sustainability series to explore AI and accessibility — how assistive tech, real-time captions, Be My Eyes' AI shift and sign-language research are expanding participation, alongside the risks of bias, privacy exploitation and a cheap 'this will do' race to the bottom that abandons human support.
keyTalkingPoints: AI is merging with assistive technology: autonomous wheelchairs, AI-enhanced cochlear tools and instant image description replacing crowdsourced volunteers
Be My Eyes becoming Be My AI moved Matt — a GPT-4 tool answers in seconds what volunteers once described, though the human connection was lovely
Sign-language interpretation AI is on its way but data-starved compared with text and audio
Amy uses ChatGPT daily as a neurodivergent professional to check tone and reduce stress — and notes institutions force her to anonymize everything, limiting real utility
The danger: organizations choosing cheap AI over skilled humans for interpreting and support, creating unequal futures based on who can pay

jimmy: Assistive AI has huge potential positives — new applications will enhance accessibility massively
Regulation is needed for assistive tools specifically, but overreach is a risk
The core risks around data and disability are the same everywhere, only more acute
matt: He was genuinely moved by Be My Eyes' shift from human volunteers to AI — instant help beats queued humans, even if something is lost
Privacy is a massive concern: assistive tech collects sensitive health and identity data that insurers could exploit
Regulation must target frontier-model development, not just how models are used
The CrowdStrike-style outage shows vulnerable people get nothing when electronic systems fail
